title: Specific Heat Capacity (c) - Definition & Key Values
topicTitle: Specific heat capacity (c) - definition and key values
notes: **Definition:** Specific heat capacity ($c$) is the amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of **1 kg** (SI) or **1 g** (CGS) of a substance by **1 K** (or 1°C). It is an intrinsic property of the material.
**Formula:** From $H = mc\Delta\theta$, solving for $c$: **$c = \frac{H}{m \cdot \Delta\theta}$**. This shows $c$ is the heat per unit mass per unit temperature change.

**Water - the benchmark:** $c_{water} = 4186\text{ J/kg·K}$ (more precisely 4181.3 J/kg·K at 15°C, but 4200 J/kg·K is standard for exam work). This is unusually high compared to most substances, making water an excellent thermal buffer.

**Ice vs. liquid water:** $c_{ice} \approx 2100\text{ J/kg·K}$ - about HALF of liquid water's specific heat. This means ice heats up twice as fast as liquid water for the same mass. During melting, the $c$ changes discontinuously.

**Metals - low specific heats:** Copper: $c = 390\text{ J/kg·K}$, Aluminum: $c = 900\text{ J/kg·K}$, Iron: $c = 450\text{ J/kg·K}$, Lead: $c = 130\text{ J/kg·K}$, Gold: $c = 129\text{ J/kg·K}$. Low $c$ means metals respond quickly to heating - useful for cookware, bad for thermal storage.

**Solids (Dulong-Petit Law):** For most solid elements at room temperature, $c \times M \approx 25\text{ J/mol·K}$ (molar heat capacity). So $c \approx 25/M$ where $M$ is molar mass in kg/mol. Heavy atoms → low $c$ per kg; light atoms → high $c$ per kg.

**Liquids:** Water: 4186, Ethanol: 2440, Mercury: 140, Glycerin: 2430, Ammonia (liquid): 4700. Gases have two specific heats ($c_p$ and $c_v$); most liquids have only one since they don't expand significantly.

**Gases - two specific heats:** For gases, $c_p > c_v$ always. At constant pressure, gas expands and does work, needing MORE heat for the same temperature rise. For air: $c_p = 1005\text{ J/kg·K}$, $c_v = 718\text{ J/kg·K}$. Ratio $\gamma = c_p/c_v \approx 1.4$.

**Temperature dependence:** Specific heat capacity is NOT truly constant - it varies with temperature. For water, $c$ changes from 4217 J/kg·K at 0°C to 4181 J/kg·K at 15°C to 4219 J/kg·K at 100°C. For most school problems, treat $c$ as constant.

**Molar heat capacity vs. specific heat:** Molar heat capacity $C_m = c \times M$ (where $M$ = molar mass). For water: $C_m = 4186 \times 0.018 = 75.3\text{ J/mol·K}$. This is useful for comparing substances on a per-molecule basis.

**Why specific heat differs:** The specific heat depends on how energy is distributed among molecular degrees of freedom. Monatomic gases store energy only in translation (3 DOF). Diatomic gases also store in rotation (2 DOF). Polyatomic molecules add vibration. More ways to store energy → higher $c$.

**Water's anomalous value:** Water's $c = 4186$ is about 5× that of copper and 10× that of lead. This is because water molecules form hydrogen bonds that must be partially broken before molecules can move faster (higher temperature). This "hidden" energy cost makes $c$ high.

**Practical - mixing two substances:** When a hot substance (mass $m_1$, $c_1$, $T_1$) is mixed with a cold substance ($m_2$, $c_2$, $T_2$), the equilibrium temperature is: $T_{eq} = \frac{m_1 c_1 T_1 + m_2 c_2 T_2}{m_1 c_1 + m_2 c_2}$. This is a weighted average by heat capacity.

**NEB focus:** Know the formula $H = mc\Delta\theta$, the values of $c$ for water and common metals, the distinction between $c$ and heat capacity ($C = mc$), and unit conversion between J/kg·K and cal/g·°C ($1\text{ J/kg·K} = 0.000239\text{ cal/g·°C}$).

**Common misconception:** "Specific" means "per unit mass" - it does NOT mean "typical" or "usual." Specific heat capacity is a very specific property that varies enormously between materials. Gold ($c=129$) and water ($c=4186$) differ by a factor of 32.
confusion: ❌ Specific heat capacity is the same for all states of a substance. ✅ Ice ($c=2100$), liquid water ($c=4186$), and steam ($c=2010$) all have different specific heats. The value changes at phase transitions.

❌ Specific heat depends on the shape/size of the object. ✅ Specific heat is an INTENSIVE property - it depends only on the material, not on the object's shape, size, or mass. A gold ring and a gold bar have the same $c$.

❌ $c_p$ and $c_v$ are the same for all substances. ✅ For solids and liquids, $c_p \approx c_v$ because they barely expand. For gases, $c_p > c_v$ significantly because gases expand and do work. The difference is $c_p - c_v = R/M$ (per kg) or $R$ (per mole).

❌ A substance with high specific heat is always "hotter." ✅ High $c$ means the substance RESISTS temperature change - it takes a lot of heat to raise its temperature. Water at 20°C has high $c$ but isn't "hot" - it just requires a lot of energy to change its temperature.

❌ The specific heat of water is 1 cal/g·°C everywhere. ✅ The calorie is DEFINED using water's specific heat, but that specific heat varies slightly with temperature. At 15°C, $c = 4.1855\text{ J/g·K}$ (giving 1 cal = 4.1855 J). The modern exact value is $1\text{ cal} = 4.184\text{ J}$ (thermochemical calorie).

❌ Gases have only one specific heat capacity. ✅ Gases have TWO: $c_p$ (constant pressure) and $c_v$ (constant volume). $c_p - c_v = R$ per mole, or $c_p - c_v = R/M$ per unit mass. For air, $c_p = 1005$ and $c_v = 718\text{ J/kg·K}$.

❌ Metals always have low specific heat. ✅ While most metals do have low $c$ (because they're dense and atoms are heavy), beryllium ($c = 1825$) and lithium ($c = 3580$) are exceptions - they have low atomic mass, so per kg they have many atoms and high heat capacity.
practice: What is the specific heat capacity of a metal if 500 J raises 0.2 kg by 10°C? $c = H/(m\Delta\theta) = 500/(0.2 \times 10) = 500/2 = 250\text{ J/kg·K}$. This matches lead or gold.

How much heat is needed to raise 3 kg of aluminum from 20°C to 100°C? $H = mc\Delta\theta = 3 \times 900 \times 80 = 216{,}000\text{ J} = 216\text{ kJ}$. Compare: same mass of water would need $3 \times 4200 \times 80 = 1{,}008{,}000\text{ J}$ - nearly 5× more!

Find the equilibrium temperature when 0.5 kg of copper ($c=390$) at 90°C is mixed with 0.2 kg of water ($c=4200$) at 20°C. $0.5 \times 390 \times (90-T) = 0.2 \times 4200 \times (T-20)$. $195(90-T) = 840(T-20)$. $17550 - 195T = 840T - 16800$. $1035T = 34350 \Rightarrow T \approx 33.2°\text{C}$.

A 0.1 kg metal at 100°C is dropped into 0.3 kg of water at 15°C. The equilibrium is 18°C. Find the metal's specific heat. Heat lost by metal: $0.1 \times c \times 82 = 8.2c$. Heat gained by water: $0.3 \times 4200 \times 3 = 3780$. $8.2c = 3780 \Rightarrow c \approx 461\text{ J/kg·K}$ (close to iron).

Why does a coastal city have smaller temperature swings than an inland city? Water has $c = 4186\text{ J/kg·K}$ - about 5× that of sand/rock ($\sim 800$). The ocean absorbs/releases enormous heat with minimal temperature change, moderating the nearby air temperature through convection and wind.
Convert 0.5 cal/g·°C to J/kg·K. $0.5\text{ cal/g·°C} \times 4.184\text{ J/cal} \times 1000\text{ g/kg} = 2092\text{ J/kg·K}$. The factor 1000 comes from g→kg; the factor 4.184 from cal→J.
universalFacts: The Dulong-Petit law (1819) states that molar heat capacity of most solid elements is approximately $3R = 24.9\text{ J/mol·K}$ at room temperature. This arises because each atom in a solid has 6 quadratic degrees of freedom (3 kinetic + 3 potential), each contributing $\frac{1}{2}k_BT$.

Water's specific heat is the highest of any common liquid. This is due to hydrogen bonding - energy goes into partially breaking H-bonds before molecules can move faster. This property is why Earth's oceans store vast amounts of solar energy.

Mercury has one of the lowest specific heats among liquids ($c = 140\text{ J/kg·K}$). This is why mercury thermometers respond quickly to temperature changes - they need very little heat to change temperature.

The concept of "thermal inertia" in climate science comes directly from specific heat. Land has lower thermal inertia than ocean, so continents heat and cool faster. This drives monsoon patterns and sea breezes.
Historical note: The word "calorimeter" comes from Latin "calor
(heat). Antoine Lavoisier built the first ice calorimeter in 1780
measuring heat by the amount of ice melted. This was the first quantitative calorimetry.
summary: Specific heat capacity c is the heat required to raise the temperature of unit mass of a substance by 1 K, so it follows directly from H = mcΔθ as c = H/(m·Δθ). It is an intensive property fixed by the material alone, which is why 1 kg and 1 g of copper share the same value of 390 J/kg·K. Water is the benchmark at about 4186 J/kg·K (4200 J/kg·K is the standard exam figure), far above every common metal, because hydrogen bonds must be partly broken before the molecules can move faster. Ice at 2100 J/kg·K and steam at 2010 J/kg·K show that c changes discontinuously at a phase boundary, and gases carry two values, c_p and c_v, with c_p > c_v always. Comparing materials in practice, when two bodies are mixed the equilibrium temperature is the heat-capacity-weighted average T_eq = (m₁c₁T₁ + m₂c₂T₂)/(m₁c₁ + m₂c₂).
importantConcepts: Definition of c as the heat per unit mass per unit temperature rise, obtained by rearranging H = mcΔθ to c = H/(m·Δθ).
Intensity: c depends only on the material, never on how much of the material is present, so 1 kg and 1 g of the same substance have identical c.
Water as the reference substance, c = 4186 J/kg·K (4200 J/kg·K in exam work), about 5 times that of copper and 10 times that of lead.
Dulong-Petit law for solid elements: the molar heat capacity c × M ≈ 25 J/mol·K, so c ≈ 25/M and heavy atoms give a low c per kilogram.
Two specific heats for gases, c_p and c_v, with c_p > c_v because a gas that expands at constant pressure must do work on its surroundings.
The equilibrium temperature of two mixed bodies, a weighted average in which the weights are the heat capacities m₁c₁ and m₂c₂, not the masses alone.
importantStatements: The specific heat capacity of a substance is the quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of that substance by 1 K.
Since c is an intensive property it does not change with the mass of the body, and it is positive for all ordinary materials.
The specific heat of a given substance is different in different states: ice 2100, liquid water 4186 and steam 2010 J/kg·K.
For every gas the specific heat at constant pressure exceeds that at constant volume, so c_p − c_v = R/M per unit mass.
When two bodies at different temperatures are mixed in an isolated system, the common final temperature is the heat-capacity-weighted average of the initial temperatures.
importantTasks: Determine the specific heat capacity of an unknown metal from the heat supplied, the mass and the measured temperature rise.
Predict the equilibrium temperature of two bodies mixed together, using c to convert each mass into a heat capacity.
Identify a substance from a tabulated specific heat value, and justify the identification by comparing orders of magnitude rather than exact figures.
Convert a specific heat capacity between J/kg·K and cal/g·°C and use it correctly inside mcΔθ.
keyPoints: c = H/(mΔθ) is the rearrangement to memorise; H = mcΔθ is the form used in numericals.
Water's c = 4186 J/kg·K is anomalously high because of hydrogen bonding, which is why oceans moderate climate.
Metals respond quickly to heating because c is small, which makes them good cookware and poor thermal storage.
Ice has roughly half the c of liquid water, so ice warms about twice as fast for the same mass and heating.
c varies slightly with temperature in reality, but school problems treat it as a constant of the material.
specialNotes: The specific heat of a substance is not the same in every state: ice 2100, liquid water 4186 and steam 2010 J/kg·K, and c jumps discontinuously at the phase boundary.
Beryllium (1825 J/kg·K) and lithium (3580 J/kg·K) are exceptions to the rule that metals have low c, because their atomic masses are small so each kilogram holds very many atoms.

The calorie was originally defined as the heat needed to raise 1 g of water by 1 °C, specifically over 14.5 °C to 15.5 °C, but water's c is not perfectly constant, so the modern exact value is 1 cal = 4.184 J.
Mercury has an exceptionally low c of 140 J/kg·K, which is why mercury thermometers respond so quickly to a change in temperature.
Liquids have essentially one specific heat because they barely expand, whereas every gas has two; writing c without a subscript for a gas is incomplete.
examShortTricks: Convert masses to kg and use c = 4200 J/kg·K for water in one step: Q in kJ equals kg × °C, a useful 3-mark shortcut.
Order-of-magnitude matching beats memorising every value: a result near 390 is copper, near 900 aluminium, near 450 iron, near 130 lead.
For a mixing problem, compute the heat capacities m₁c₁ and m₂c₂ first and treat them as the weights; a mass-weighted average is almost always wrong.
The single conversion 1 cal/g·°C = 4184 J/kg·K absorbs both the calorie factor and the gram-to-kilogram factor.
examNotes: Two to three mark numericals on finding an unknown c from a heated block or a cooling curve appear in most papers.
The mixing formula is a regular 5 mark question, often with a copper or aluminium block dropped into water and the equilibrium temperature measured.
One-mark recall questions ask for the specific heat of water in SI and CGS units, and for the definition of specific heat capacity as an intensive property.
Expect a comparison question: why water is used as a coolant, or why a coastal city has smaller temperature swings than an inland one.
practiceQuestions: A metal receives 500 J and its 0.2 kg mass rises by 10 °C. What is its specific heat capacity, and which metal does it suggest?
How much heat is needed to raise 3 kg of aluminium from 20 °C to 100 °C, and how does this compare with the same mass of water?
Find the equilibrium temperature when 0.5 kg of copper at 90 °C is mixed with 0.2 kg of water at 20 °C.
A 0.1 kg metal at 100 °C dropped into 0.3 kg of water at 15 °C gives an equilibrium of 18 °C. Identify the metal.
Convert 0.215 cal/g·°C into J/kg·K and account for both factors in the conversion.
